content.intro: This lesson develops topic 35 of the supplied curriculum: **Indexing One-Dimensional Arrays**. The main starting point is **Reading individual values**. You will connect the idea to a small, synthetic example, then use the result to reason about shape, dtype, accuracy, or memory as appropriate.
content.why_it_matters: Indexing is the boundary between an array's full dataset and the values a calculation should use. Explicit row/column thinking helps avoid selecting the wrong axis.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat **Indexing One-Dimensional Arrays** as an explicit step in an array workflow. This lesson centers on **Reading individual values** and the source syllabus's related subtopics. Before trusting a result, identify the input shape and dtype, perform the smallest useful operation, and inspect the output. The example uses synthetic data so you can change one value and observe what changes.

import numpy as np

values = np.array([10, 20, 30])
values[1] = 99
print(values)

common_mistakes.problem: Using separate row and column assumptions for 1D data
common_mistakes.why: A vector has one axis; it does not have independent row/column indexes.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the shape and use a consistent axis convention.

common_mistakes.problem: Expecting advanced indexing to behave like a slice
common_mistakes.why: Integer-array indexing generally returns a copy.
